nameStory: Bird's-eye speedwell gets its charming name from its tiny bright blue flowers with darker lines that look like miniature bird eyes peering up at you from the ground. The 'speedwell' part comes from an old tradition of pinning these flowers to travelers' clothes as a good luck charm, wishing them to 'speed well' on their journeys.
description: Bird's-eye speedwell is a low-growing annual plant that forms small mats close to the ground, rarely getting taller than your ankle. It produces tiny but brilliant blue flowers with four petals that seem almost too bright for such a small plant. The flowers are only about a quarter-inch across, but their vivid sky-blue color with darker radiating lines makes them surprisingly eye-catching when you notice them carpeting disturbed soil in early spring.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright blue flowers with four petals and darker blue lines radiating from the center like spokes on a wheel, sitting on thin stalks that emerge from where leaves meet the stem

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves with slightly toothed edges that feel soft and somewhat fuzzy to the touch, arranged in opposite pairs along the creeping stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low spreading mats that hug the ground, with stems that trail along the soil surface and root at joints, creating small colonies

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, heart-shaped seed capsules that split open to reveal tiny brown seeds, often with a small notch at the top

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves have a distinctive fresh, slightly bitter smell when crushed between your fingers, and the plant has an overall soft, delicate texture

habitat: Bird's-eye speedwell thrives in disturbed soils like garden beds, lawn edges, pathways, and cultivated areas throughout New England. You'll often find it in slightly moist, nutrient-rich soil where other plants have been disturbed, making it common around homes, farms, and parks. It particularly loves areas with partial shade to full sun where the soil stays somewhat loose and fertile.

seasonality.spring: This is when bird's-eye speedwell truly shines, producing its brilliant blue flowers from March through May and creating small carpets of color in disturbed ground.
seasonality.summer: Plants continue flowering into early summer but become less noticeable as other vegetation grows taller, though you can still find the distinctive heart-shaped seed capsules.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline and set seed for next year's crop, with the heart-shaped capsules splitting open to release tiny seeds.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate when warm weather returns.

funFact: Despite being called 'Persian speedwell,' this little plant is actually a master of global conquest - it has successfully colonized every continent except Antarctica, all within the last 200 years, making it one of the most successful plant travelers in modern history.
confusionNotes: Bird's-eye speedwell is most easily confused with other small blue-flowered speedwells, but its four-petaled bright blue flowers with dark lines are distinctive - most other speedwells have paler blue or white flowers. Remember: if the tiny blue flowers look like bright bird eyes staring up at you, you've found the right speedwell.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'Persian speedwell' and native to Eurasia, this plant was first recorded in Britain in 1825 and has since become naturalized across much of North America. It's considered a non-native species but is generally not invasive enough to cause major ecological problems.
compareHints: Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines. While thyme-leaved speedwell has pale blue or white flowers and corn speedwell has tiny inconspicuous flowers, bird's-eye speedwell's flowers are distinctly vibrant and eye-catching. Its four-petaled flowers are also slightly larger than most of its close relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
